933.dq: Stress is contrastive in Bantoanon words. ... [1.3] The pause group serves as the matrix for the stress group. The nucleus of a pause group is a stress group which carries more intensity than the other stress groups. Slightly higher pitch usually accompanies intensity.
933.dloc: Kilgour & Hendrickson 1992 sec. 1.4 'Stress group' (p.113); sec. 1.3 'Pause group' (p.112)
933.prule: Contrastive (phonemic, lexical) word stress in Bantoanon within a right-edge two-syllable window ('Primary stress favours the penultimate or ultimate syllable'), with minimal pairs túkub/tukúb, kítaq/kitá, qúbus/qubús, sípit/sipít; realized as vowel length in open stressed syllables (word-final open stressed V has [h]-like breathiness) and as loudness in closed ones; optional secondary stress two syllables before the primary. Zorc 1977's pan-Bisayan comparative statement agrees (phonemic penult/ultima accent retained in all Bs varieties incl. Ban). NOTE: Zorc's pan-Bisayan sub-rule 'a closed penult is stressed' (8.10.2, 3.1.3) is NOT borne out for Bantoanon in the Banton-specific primary, which transcribes closed-penult words with ultimate stress ([sak.'yan] /sakyán/ 'ride', [pak.'lɩs] /paklís/ 'peeling skin', [tug.'rok] /tugrúk/ 'build', p.121) alongside penult-stressed ones (/gúlpi/, /pálta/, /párti/, /súnrang/, /púnla/, p.133); so no weight sub-regularity is coded.
933.srule: Optional secondary stress on the second syllable before the primary-stressed syllable (["sa.lum.'pa:.ti] 'dove'), with the same but weaker cues as primary stress; in full-base reduplications secondary stress usually stays on the base's stressed syllable while primary moves to the penult of the reduplicated form ([ba."yay.'ba:.yay] 'playhouse').

935.dq: Se observan restricciones en el sistema tonal BAS: no hay palabras de tono B mientras que sí las hay de tono A; hay por lo menos un tono A (Gomez-Imbert 2004-05: 69); Jones & Jones 1991: 10 'Stress is phonemic on the word level, with one primary stress per word.'
935.dloc: Gomez-Imbert 2004-05 sec. 5 'Tonalidad' p. 67 through sec. 5.1 'Tonos lexicos' pp. 68-69 (quote); sec. 2.1 p. 49 (moraic weight has no accentual role); fn. 37 p. 76 (on Jones & Jones). Jones & Jones 1991 sec. 1.14 'Stress and pitch', pp. 10-13 (archive.org excerpt pp. 2-5).
935.prule: No stress rule. Barasana is described (Gomez-Imbert 2004-05) as a restricted two-tone system (Alto/Bajo = H/L), tone-bearing unit the mora, with only two lexical tonal specifications per root (/A/=H and /AB/=HL), each with a subclass whose initial mora is extratonal (surface initial L inserted by default); every word has at least one H, there are no all-L words and no initial LL. The author states the system can be analysed either as tone or as pitch accent ('acento tonal') and prefers the tonal analysis; tone also carries central grammatical functions (tonal prefixes on the verb, sec. 5.2). Jones & Jones 1991 describe the same facts as 'phonemic stress' = the first high-pitched syllable of the word (prenuclear syllables low, postnuclear H or L by morpheme), lexically contrastive (rii 'blood' vs rii 'meat', accents lost in scan) and differing lexically between Barasano and Taiwano/Eduria; either way the position of the prominence/first H is lexical, not computable from syllable count or weight.
935.srule: Not mentioned in Gomez-Imbert 2004-05 (sec. 5-5.2, pp. 67-73 read; tonal analysis: within the word A+AB is kept, AB+A -> AB, AB+AB -> AB; in compounds the first constituent's tone dominates). The only secondary-stress statement is Jones & Jones 1991 sec. 1.14 (pp. 12-13), placed by morphology: class-2 verb suffixes (e.g. -bosa 'benefactive') carry a secondary stress with high pitch after the root's primary stress; class-3 verb suffixes (negative -beti, proximate -di) take the primary stress, leaving secondary stress on the root. Gomez-Imbert & Kenstowicz 2000 (sec. 4.2, 7) reanalyse this tonally: one pitch peak per word/accentual domain, long words splitting into two domains each with its own peak; no rhythmic secondary stress in any source.

935.tone: Gomez-Imbert 2004-05 (fieldwork 1984-98): 'son sistemas de dos tonos, alto y bajo'; TBU = mora; lexical classes /A/ vs /AB/ (+ extratonal-initial subclasses); at least one H per word; optional final lengthening of <B>AB nouns taken as evidence 'de la presencia de tonos subyacentes (y no de un acento)'; system 'puede ser analizado, tanto como un sistema tonal como un sistema de acento tonal (pitch accent)', pitch-accent analysis in Gomez-Imbert 1997a and Gomez-Imbert & Kenstowicz 2000 (IJAL 66.4, 'Barasana Tone and Accent'), tonal analysis preferred since Gomez-Imbert 1999/2001. On weight (p. 49): 'El peso moráico no tiene el impacto que suele tener en lenguas acentuales como el latín pero permite, por ejemplo, ubicar fronteras morfémicas como en ríá-gá, por hallarse las sílabas bimoráicas en posición final de morfema.' On Jones & Jones 1991 (fn. 37): 'Estos autores ignoran totalmente las V largas y los tonos, que nunca transcriben, lo cual hace que el BAS que ellos describen parece ser un idioma distinto del que yo describo. Pero no lo es, pues hemos tenido al menos una consultante principal en común, Hilda Marín, quien pronuncia claramente V largas y tonos.' Jones & Jones 1991 themselves call it phonemic word stress whose correlates are 'high pitch, loudness, long vowel, and sometimes a fortis consonant', the stressed syllable being 'the first high-pitched syllable' and admit 'the presence of phonemic stress and/or high pitch is difficult to determine'.

935.sec_quote: Verb suffixes fall into three classes: 1. Those which have low pitch. (This is the more general case.) 2. Those which pull the stress to themselves, hence carrying secondary stress. 3. The class three verb suffixes carry the primary word stress, leaving secondary stress on the root.

939.prule: Default: primary stress on the penult of the word, moving to the new penult under suffixation (dálan 'road', mardálan, dalánna, pardalaníɔn 'journey'). Final (ultima) stress is assigned by grammatical/morphological class: predicative adjectives ('group VII modifiers') vs. the corresponding noun or verb (tíbbo 'height' vs tibbó 'high'; gájjaŋ 'length' vs gajjáŋ 'long'; lápu 'to smear' vs lapú 'be smeared') — 'innumerable examples... no exceptions'; vocatives (ínaŋ 'mother' vs ináŋ 'mother!'); comparatives in -an; excessive adjectives in -hu; honorific enclitic -mu forms (taŋammú, hamú); prefixed derivatives of monosyllabic roots (mardúm, pasíp); plus recent loans (ekonomí, parlemén). Author calls stress 'distinctive and hence... a phoneme'.
939.srule: Word-level non-primary stress (Nababan's 'tertiary'; he reserves 'secondary' for emphatic phrase-level prominence) on the word-initial syllable when it is neither the penult nor the antepenult (bòrunámi, pàrborúɔn, pàrdalaníɔn); in longer words a further tertiary two or three syllables before the primary (pàrborùɔnnámi, pàrborùɔnnasída, pàrdalanìɔnnasída), the spacing 'not absolute'; none in di- and trisyllables (bóru, parbóru).

940.dloc: van der Tuuk 1864, Eerste stuk: Inleiding III (dialects; Angkola = noord-Mandailingsch, p. IV); Tobasch klankstelsel par. 18 'De Klemtoon' p.18 (scan leaf 35), par. 19 'Plaats van den klemtoon' p.19 (leaf 36), par. 20 p.20 (leaf 37), Aanm. 1-2 p.21 (leaf 38); Mandailingsch klankstelsel H p.31 (leaf 48): 'De klemtoon is hier als in T.'
940.prule: Stress (klemtoon) falls on the final or the penultimate syllable (right-edge two-syllable window: daó, bóltok, debatá, sibórang); which of the two is not computable from syllable count: 'not yet determinable here, since the place of the stress depends not only on the class the word belongs to but also on its function in the sentence' (par. 19). Provisional rules: substantives as a rule penult (bíjang, bóltok); exceptions = loans and words whose final syllable has a contracted vowel (debatá, suttorá, sukkurá; 'how narumó comes by its stress I do not know'); monosyllabic pronouns attract the stress (the preceding word keeps a half-stress); the interjection alé and address forms have final stress (alé radjanamí, alé amák); intransitives with final stress (daó) mostly go penult after na/ma (nadáo, madáo). 'For many words the stress is arbitrary and cannot be brought under a rule', with meaning pairs: sogot 'at some (future) time' vs sogót 'early in the morning'; paulá 'pretend' vs paula 'make work'. Mandailing (incl. noord-Mandailingsch = Angkola) is stated to have stress 'as in Toba' (p.31 H).
940.srule: Half stress (van der Tuuk 1864 par. 18 a, stated for Toba; Mandailing/Angkola 'stress as in Toba', p.31): words of more than three syllables are pronounced almost as two words, divided so that the last part has three syllables when the count is odd; only the last part has the full stress, the first part a half stress in the same relative position (gàbe-bólon, dàrambanúwa, dumàredé, pàbowàhonókkon). Words of up to three syllables: no secondary stress described. Dongoran et al. 1997 (Angkola data, pp.149-150) grade all pretonic syllables as equal secondary and the final as weakest: 2-1-3, 2-2-1-3, 2-2-2-1-3.

dqtr.text: [Toba sec. 20 Aanm. 2, p.21, general statement for Batak] Batak knows only the syllable accent (lettergreep-toon) within a word. Word stress (woord-klemtoon), by which one lays emphasis on a word in the sentence, is unknown there.

942.heavy: syllables with ĕ (toonlooze/kleurlooze klinker, schwa) are light: stress passes from an ĕ-syllable to the next syllable (a final closed ĕ-syllable after another ĕ-syllable does carry the stress, bĕlĕ́n); a 'gerekte klinker' (lengthened/contracted vowel) in the final syllable is heavy and takes the stress
942.dflt: not stated outright. By Dairi V ('In een ligtste lettergreep moet deze tongval ĕ hebben') together with Toba sec. 18's definition of 'ligtste' as the unstressed penult, a full-vowel penult implies penult stress, so words with no ĕ and no long final vowel come out penult; van der Tuuk himself only says the Toba rules (final or penult by word class/function, substantives as a rule penult, many words arbitrary) lapse 'voor een groot gedeelte'.
942.prule: Dairi stress sits in the Toba-type right-edge window (final or penult) and its place is read off the vowels: a syllable containing ĕ (schwa) always passes the stress to the FOLLOWING syllable, even when that syllable itself contains ĕ (bĕlĕ́n, bĕlgáh: a final closed ĕ-syllable can thus bear stress); ĕ never stands in a final open or h-closed syllable; a lengthened (contracted) vowel in the final syllable takes the stress; conversely every 'lightest' syllable (Toba sec. 18: the unstressed penult) must have ĕ in Dairi (mĕndok = Toba mandók, bĕlgah = balgá). Hence the Toba/Mandailing placement rules (word class, syntactic function, lexically arbitrary for many words) 'voor een groot gedeelte vervallen' for Dairi. Suffix -su attracts stress (ĕntorsú); vocative stress as in Toba. Loan exception debatá (expected debĕta or dibáta; also spoken debáta).
942.srule: Half (secondary) stress is described only in the grammar's general Batak stress section, on Toba forms (van der Tuuk 1864 sec. 18a, pp.18-19): words of more than three syllables are pronounced almost as two words; only the last part (three syllables if the total is odd, otherwise two) has the full stress, and the earlier part(s) a half stress in the same position as the full stress in the last part (gàbe-bólon, dàrambanúwa, dumàredé, pàbowàhonókkon). The Dairi chapter's stress paragraph (K, p.40) neither restates nor cancels this, and Dairi avoids words of more than three syllables (III a, p.41; Adelaar 1981:5 'lexemes of more than three syllables are unusual'); no secondary-stress statement made on Dairi data exists in the works read (van der Tuuk 1864, Adelaar 1981, Sembiring et al. 1993).

943.dloc: Newell 1970, sec. 3 'The Stress Group', pp. 110-113 (stress-group nucleus = loudest syllable, p. 110; contrastive stress placement, Descriptions 1-3, pp. 111-113); sec. 0 p. 101 (stress group ~ word); sec. 4 p. 113 (pause-group stress distinct). Newell 1993 sketch sec. 4.3 for the length reanalysis.
943.prule: Contrastive (lexical) stress placement: a two-way contrast, stress on either the penult or the ultima of the word base (minimal pairs qitulud 'will push' vs qitulud 'will accompany', gayang 'hawk' vs gayang 'spear', qidew 'omen bird' vs 'a variety of snake'); enclitic pronouns and particles (one or two syllables) may follow the stressed syllable within the stress group without bearing or shifting stress. Newell's adopted analysis (Description 3) states this as two contrastive stress-group types rather than in terms of the word base, but the contrast is the same.
943.srule: None: one stress per stress group (~ word) - 'only one syllable characterized by a controlled movement contrasts in intensity with the other syllables of the stress group. This syllable is stressed; all other syllables are unstressed.' Newell describes a durational (not stress) rhythm of 'controlled' (long) vs 'ballistic' (short, clipped) syllables - pre-stress syllable ballistic, non-adjacent initial syllable controlled, odd/even alternation before the stress, post-stress syllables controlled - and explicitly declines to label controlled syllables secondary-stressed because no intensity contrast is audible outside the stressed syllable. Newell 1993 and Reid 1971 (entry 12) do not mention secondary stress.

evidence_works.detail: Dictionary front-matter phonology sketch by the same author as the record source (Newell 1970). It describes contrastive vowel LENGTH, not stress: 'Vowels are pronounced either long or short. A long vowel is approximately twice as long in duration of pronunciation as a short vowel. Length is a significant feature, often being the minimal difference between two words, e.g., gumilit "crowd each other" and gumilit "strips rice grains"' (p. 5). Position: 'Length, when it occurs, is on the second to the last vowel of a stem form, unless it is affected by affixation, e.g., muntalid "sharpens a round point". Length only occurs on vowels of open syllables. Vowels of closed syllables are always short' (p. 5). Alternation argument for the position: 'Suffixation of a stem with length by the affixes -an or -on, however, pulls the length feature to the last syllable of the stem (talid + -an = talidan...)' and talin + -an + -na = talinana (p. 5). The 'twice as long' figure is an impressionistic statement, not an instrumental measurement; no elicitation procedure is described in the excerpt.

dfl.note: The primary source states no default (stress 'lexically specified and contrastive'). Dubina 2012 argues that the East Slavic/Belarusian default, visible in nonce words and borrowings and in type counts, is fixed stem-final (root) stress = accentual pattern A; Bethin 2022: 249 likewise calls A-FIXED STEM stress 'by far the majority pattern in all nouns'. This is a majority/analytic default within a lexical system, not a positional rule counted from a word edge.
dfl.q: Apparently, the East Slavic default is not just to have a stem-final stress, it is to have a fixed stem-final stress. That the accentual pattern A, where stress is fixed on the root, is the prevailing pattern in East Slavic, is nothing particularly new. ... In Belarusian, only about 20% of masculine nouns with monosyllabic roots follow pattern C, whereas pattern A accounts for about 65%

948.heavy: closed syllables counting as heavy (bimoraic feet; no vowel-length contrast) -- relevant to secondary-stress footing only, not to the position of main stress
948.dflt: not applicable to main stress (always prosodic-word-initial); all-light words foot as syllabic trochees from the left, e.g. ('phagi)(det)(lem)
948.prule: Main (primary) stress falls on the initial syllable of the prosodic word, quantity-insensitive (an initial open syllable simply lengthens optionally under main stress; e.g. 'no.ka.tsik 'brain' with light initial). The prosodic word begins at the stem: prefixes (u- 3sgPOSS, N-, miN- NEG etc.) and clitics are outside it, except that a prefix is incorporated (and stressed) when excluding it would leave main stress on a word-final syllable ('ʔu.hop, 'min.lu).
948.srule: Secondary stress on the head of every non-initial foot: bimoraic (moraic) trochees built left to right from the main-stressed prosodic-word-initial syllable, closed syllables heavy; a light syllable that cannot be footed is skipped (no degenerate feet except under main stress) and secondary stress is blocked from final open syllables, e.g. ('noka)(cik) 'brain', ('phek)(kuli) 'buckwheat', ('labho)ka(rik) 'small bird', ('phagi)(det)(lem) 'butterfly'; suffix strings carry secondary stress only on tautomorphemic bimoraic feet.

951.tone: 1892 missionary grammar; tone is not analysed. Benga (Bantu A34) is very probably tonal like its zone-A relatives: Nassau p. 61 describes negation 'by peculiar vocal stress, difficult to be recognized or acquired by a foreigner, laid on the nominative', marked with a grave accent (an unanalysed tonal negative); Meinhof 1889/90 ('Das Zeitwort in der Benga-Sprache', Zeitschrift fuer afrikanische Sprachen III, archive.org, sect. 22) likewise says positive and negative pronominal verb forms 'sich in der Schrift ganz gleichsehen. Der Unterschied liegt jedenfalls in der Aussprache' and marks negatives with an accent, giving no accent-position rule; and the other reachable primary, Salvado y Cos 1891 (Coleccion de apuntes preliminares sobre la lengua benga, archive.org coleccindeapunt00cosgoog), reports verbs 'identicos en la escritura y no en el significado' (yaka 'dormir' vs yaka 'llorar') which 'distinguen perfectamente los bengas por medio del acento o pronunciacion' and 'Ellos saben dar tal acento a la voz, que no deja duda alguna sobre su significado' -- lexical tone minimal pairs heard as 'accent'. 955.tone: Saxena describes phonemic tone with minimal pairs (làm 'path' / lám 'shoe'; also transitivity pairs kònʤa intr / kónʤa tr); low tone = falling-rising contour with slight aspiration, high/neutral = level; contrast confined to first syllable and 'predictable to a large extent' from onset type (Tibetan-style register split); first-syllable tone spreads to the next syllable; grammatical morphemes toneless except a few verb-complex morphemes. The direct-elicited material was primarily collected from Mr. Padam Sagar, a native of the Nako village' (p. 186). Adds one sentence the 2022 chapter dropped: 'While the tonal distinction is distinctly audible in lexical items when spoken in isolation, in free speech the tonal differences are not so distinct; instead the main distinctive feature is primarily the tonal contour' (p. 190). 957.prule: Pitch (plus some intensity) accent, normally one accented syllable per word, but its position is 'relativement libre', 'assez largement imprévisible', fluctuating for the same noun between citation form, running text and speakers; no minimal pairs, no phonological status. Statistical tendencies only (citation forms of 941 nouns): accent avoids the class prefix (90%), falling on the final (53%) or penultimate (38%) syllable, 9% elsewhere. Author declines to mark accent in the rest of the grammar ('l'accent échappe pour l'instant à toute tentative de systématisation', 6.3).
957.srule: Nouns of 4+ syllables sometimes carry a secondary accent slightly lower in pitch than the main one (one-accent rule holds for 97% of nouns of 3 syllables or fewer, 84% of 4+; e.g. e-yindɔni [e-yín-dɔ-ní]). In verbs the accentual scheme of the whole form is morphologically distinctive (e.g. ɔ-ka-dá 'qu'il vienne' vs ɔ-ká-da 'il n'est pas venu'; virtual -ba always accented, with a mobile, unstable second accent: ya-bá-dá 'ils viendront' / yá-bá-da 's'ils viennent'), though also variable in context. Accent tends to fall on short vowels; lengthened (mostly penultimate, non-phonemic) vowels are rarely accented.

957.tone: Author weighs a tonal analysis (6.1.1, 6.1.5) and rejects it synchronically: at most one contrastively high syllable per short noun, no all-H/all-L schemes, no minimal pairs in Bubaque, large citation/context variation; suggests the system may be the degradation of an older tone system (sporadic minimal pairs reported for other lects, e.g. Canhabaque ni-gigí 'talon' vs ní-gígí 'mil noir', the latter an all-H scheme unknown at Bubaque); probable downdrift of successive accented syllables.

957.sec_rule: Exists but unplaced: citation-form nouns normally carry one accent (97% of nouns of <=3 syllables, 84% of nouns of 4+ syllables); nouns of 4+ syllables sometimes carry a secondary accent slightly lower in pitch than the main accent (ex. e-yindɔni [e-yín-dɔ-ní]); no rule for its position is given. 958.prule: Lexical (contrastive, unpredictable) stress on either the penultimate or the final syllable of polysyllabic words (a two-syllable window at the right edge), independent of a culminative word-final lexical tone contrast (High ³ / Extra-High ⁴ / toneless). Arnold 2025 sec. 4.1: 'Stress, on the other hand, falls unpredictably on either the penultimate or final syllable of polysyllabic words in all varieties' (the five Maˈya dialects and Biga); Table 7 (Biga): ˈbaybu⁴k 'blunt' vs baˈbu⁴s 'white', ˈmana³ 'light (weight)' vs maˈme³ 'red', kaˈwat 'root'; Table 9 row 1 'Contrastive stress: penultimate vs final' Biga = Y. Stated regularities: a strong tendency for penultimately stressed words to have identical penultimate and final vowels (kaˈmumu³s 'mosquito', ˈbini³s 'hot', maˈnyana³m 'sharp'); no tone restriction on penultimately stressed words in Biga (unlike the Maˈya dialects); toneless words with penultimate stress not attested; no phrase-medial apocope in Biga. Phonetic correlates of stress (duration, vowel quality, intensity) are reported only for Salawati Maˈya (Remijsen 2001a: 54-68). No fixed-stress rule (quantity-insensitive); no rule string.

958.tone: Lexical tone AND lexical stress, analysed as independent systems (Arnold 2025 sec. 4.1, following Remijsen 2001a/b, 2002 and van der Leeden 1993 for Maˈya). Tone is culminative ('a maximum of on [sic: one] tone per word') and restricted to the word-final syllable; Biga contrasts High (³) and Extra-High (⁴) with toneless syllables (Table 5: du³n 'fish' / ‑bu⁴n 'to kill' / ‑un 'to know'; lu³ 'sea' / lu⁴ 'two'; ɪ³f 'island' / ɪ⁴s 'dog'; la³p 'fire' / lap 'body.3SG'); toneless words optionally take prepausal epenthetic /‑o/. Unlike the Maˈya dialects, Biga has no restriction on which tone combines with penultimate stress (ˈlomo³s 'blood', ‑ˈama³t 'to burn' High; ‑ˈini⁴m 'to drink', kaˈbutu⁴ 'cold' Extra-High), but toneless penultimately stressed words are unattested (Table 7). Diachrony (sec. 4.2, ms p.17): Biga is an offshoot of Kawe (Waigeo) Maˈya with two innovations, PWM *ˈσ³ > Biga ˈσ⁴ and PWM *ˈσ¹² > Biga ˈσ³. Corroborated: Arnold, Gao & Kirby 2023 ICPhS sec. 1.2 ('in Biga, the contrast is between High, Extra-High, and toneless syllables'; 'generally culminative and limited to word-final syllables'); Arnold 2020: 27-28 (generic over Salawati/Batta/Biga/As); Arnold ICHL26 abstract ('two... underlying tones on word final syllables'); Remijsen 2001: 158 ('Biga may well feature a tone contrast with a limited lexical load').
